title: ZK Engineering Lab — Build a ZK App End to End

questions.question: What is the purpose of binding a ZK proof to a server-provided session challenge (e.g., a session_id)?
options: To prevent replaying an old proof as a fresh login attempt
To make the proof shorter
To avoid using a hash function in Fiat–Shamir
To hide the public key from the verifier
questions.explanation: Without a unique challenge, a captured (valid) proof can be replayed to authenticate again. Binding the proof to a per-session message makes replays fail.

questions.question: What does "domain separation" mean when hashing a proof transcript?
options: Including a protocol-specific label so the same bytes cannot be interpreted as a challenge in a different protocol
Using a different prime modulus for each user
Running the hash twice to double security
Encrypting the transcript before hashing
questions.explanation: A domain tag (and/or transcript context) prevents cross-protocol confusion where the same byte string is accepted in multiple roles or protocols.

questions.question: In Schnorr NIZK, the verifier checks g^s == R · pk^c (mod p). Why must the verifier also validate that pk is in the correct subgroup?
options: To prevent small-subgroup / invalid-element attacks that can break soundness or leak information
Because pk validation makes the proof smaller
Because pk must be equal to g
Because Fiat–Shamir only works for prime fields of size 2^k
questions.explanation: If pk is not a valid subgroup element, algebraic checks may succeed for unintended reasons. Group membership checks are part of making the proof system sound in an application.

questions.question: Why do we hash (p, q, g, pk, R, message) — not just (R, message) — to compute the Fiat–Shamir challenge c?
options: It binds the proof to the exact statement and parameters, reducing cross-protocol and cross-parameter confusion
It makes SHA-256 faster by adding more input bytes
It hides the value R from the verifier
It ensures c is never 0
questions.explanation: Including parameters and statement data makes the challenge unambiguous and protocol-specific, so the same transcript bytes cannot be reused under different assumptions.

questions.question: Two valid proofs reuse the same nonce (same R) but have different challenges c1 ≠ c2. What can an attacker compute?
options: The secret x via x = (s1 - s2) · (c1 - c2)^{-1} mod q
A new generator g
A collision in SHA-256
Nothing — nonce reuse is safe in Schnorr proofs
questions.explanation: From s1 = r + c1x and s2 = r + c2x, subtract to eliminate r and solve for x. This is the classic nonce-reuse failure mode.

questions.question: Why is length-prefixed encoding (e.g., u16 || bytes) used in transcript hashing?
options: To avoid ambiguity where different tuples of values serialize to the same byte string
To make integers constant-time
To make SHA-256 output longer
To ensure the proof is zero-knowledge
questions.explanation: Without a canonical, unambiguous encoding, an attacker can exploit parser/serializer mismatches or concatenation ambiguity to change what is being proven.

questions.question: A server verifies a proof but does not track whether a (user_id, session_id) was already used. What bug does this introduce?
options: Replay: the same proof can be reused to mint multiple tokens for the same session
Soundness: g^s == R · pk^c no longer holds
Completeness: honest proofs start failing randomly
Confidentiality: the secret x becomes public immediately
questions.explanation: Even a correct proof system needs application-level state to prevent replays. Otherwise a captured proof for that session can be reused.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the boundary between "crypto correctness" and "app correctness" in a ZK login flow?
options: Crypto correctness proves the statement; app correctness ensures the statement is the right one (fresh, bound, authorized) and is used safely
If the proof verifies, the app is automatically secure
App correctness is irrelevant because ZK proofs are zero-knowledge
Crypto correctness only matters if the server stores the secret key
questions.explanation: A proof can be valid yet useless or dangerous if it proves the wrong thing or can be replayed. Engineering is about correctly binding proofs to intent and state.
